Vegetation classification: a phytosociological approach

Marco Pittarello

Source: vignettes/TUTORIAL_3_-_Cluster_metodo_fitosociologico.Rmd
TUTORIAL_3_-_Cluster_metodo_fitosociologico.Rmd

This vignette illustrates classification using modified TWINSPAN and selection of the number of groups using OptimClass. The resulting groups are then described using Indicator Species Analysis (ISA), the phi coefficient, tb-PCA, and a synoptic table.

The example uses only iPastoralist::data. For this example, survey values are assumed to represent percentage cover, although the demonstration dataset was originally organised as frequencies of occurrence. This assumption illustrates the workflow; it is not a methodological conversion from FO to cover. Real applications require observed cover values and careful consideration of the measurement scale.

1. Required packages and functions

TWINSPAN requires a version of ecan that exports twinspan().

library(iPastoralist)
library(vegan)
library(indicspecies)
library(permute)

2. Preparing cover data 

data_example <- as.data.frame(iPastoralist::data)
data_example <- data_example[, c(2, 7:30)]

cover <- iPastoralist::vegetation_abundance(
  database = data_example,
  species.cover.coefficient = 4,
  method = "SC_fo_occ"
)

# Rows = surveys; columns = species.
veg <- t(cover)

dim(veg)
#> [1]  24 152
knitr::kable(veg[seq_len(min(6L, nrow(veg))), seq_len(min(6L, ncol(veg)))])
Achmacr Achmill Achmosc Acialpi Acolama Adealli
R1 0 0 0 0 0.3 0.0
R2 0 0 0 0 0.0 0.3
R3 0 0 0 0 0.0 0.0
R4 0 0 0 0 0.0 0.0
R5 0 0 0 0 0.0 0.0
R6 0 0 0 0 0.0 0.0

3. Modified TWINSPAN and OptimClass

TWINSPAN uses pseudospecies cut levels to represent abundances. Here, the cover thresholds are 0, 2, 5, 10, and 20. Modified TWINSPAN prioritises splitting the most heterogeneous group. OptimClass compares partitions based on faithful species: OptimClass 1 considers the total number of faithful species, whereas OptimClass 2 considers the number of groups containing a sufficient number of faithful species (Tichý et al., 2010).

The significance threshold and minimum number of faithful species are analysis parameters that should be reported and assessed for your dataset. The range of group numbers examined here is also limited by the small size of the demonstration dataset.

min_size <- 2L
k_values <- 2:8
cut_levels <- c(0, 2, 5, 10, 20)
p_threshold <- 1e-3
min_faithful <- 3L
select_by <- "optimclass2" # alternative: "optimclass1"

In the ecan backend, min_size controls which groups can be split further; on its own, it does not guarantee that every final group contains at least that many surveys. Always check final group sizes after classification.

twinspan_res <- twinspan_optimclass_ecan(
  veg = veg,
  cut_levels = cut_levels,
  min_size = min_size,
  k_values = k_values,
  p_threshold = p_threshold,
  min_faithful = min_faithful,
  version = "fast",
  select_by = select_by,
  show_plots = TRUE
)

#> 
#> --- TWINSPAN + OPTIMCLASS ---
#> Version: fast 
#> OptimClass 1, optimal k values: 3, 4 
#> OptimClass 2, optimal k values: 3, 4 
#> Selected partition:3groups (optimclass2)
#> Unique faithful species: 4

twinspan_res$faithful_by_group

4. Selecting the partition and aligning groups

The default solution is the one returned by OptimClass. If no single valid selected_k is returned, examine results and best_k and choose a solution explicitly. For example, a maximum OptimClass 2 score of zero does not demonstrate that the groups meet the desired faithful-species requirement.

n.cluster <- twinspan_res$selected_k
groups_raw <- as.data.frame(twinspan_res$classification)

To assess an alternative solution, run the following chunk instead of the previous one. It is excluded from normal rendering with eval = FALSE to avoid automatically overwriting the OptimClass selection. After running it manually, rerun all subsequent chunks, starting with group alignment.

k_custom <- 4L

twin_ecan <- ecan::twinspan(
  x = veg,
  modified = TRUE,
  n_clusters = k_custom,
  cut_levels = cut_levels,
  min_size = min_size,
  max_depth = 6,
  polish = "hill",
  species = FALSE
)

groups_raw <- as.data.frame(twin_ecan$classification[, c("stand", "group")])
n.cluster <- length(unique(groups_raw$group))
if (n.cluster != k_custom) {
  stop("TWINSPAN did not reach the requested number of groups.")
}

# Convert using the ecan S3 method, without calling internal functions.
hc_ecan <- stats::as.hclust(twin_ecan)
plot(hc_ecan, hang = -1, sub = "", main = "TWINSPAN - alternative solution")

Retain the partition in classification: do not derive a new classification by applying cutree() to the displayed dendrogram. Recode group labels as 1, 2, etc., and store them as a factor with the same level order for ISA, phi, PCA, and the synoptic table. This ensures that the version of synoptic_table() that adds a G prefix to frequency columns produces G1, G2, etc.

groups <- groups_raw[
  match(rownames(veg), as.character(groups_raw$stand)),
  c("stand", "group"),
  drop = FALSE
]
rownames(groups) <- NULL

# Retain the mapping to the original group labels.
original_group_levels <- levels(factor(groups$group))
group_key <- data.frame(
  original_group = original_group_levels,
  group = seq_along(original_group_levels)
)
groups$group <- factor(
  match(as.character(groups$group), original_group_levels),
  levels = seq_along(original_group_levels)
)

stopifnot(
  identical(rownames(veg), as.character(groups$stand)),
  !anyNA(groups$group),
  nlevels(droplevels(groups$group)) == n.cluster
)

5. Indicator Species Analysis

Calculate IndVal from cover data, using func = "IndVal.g" to account for unequal group sizes. Setting duleg = TRUE searches for species associated with individual groups, excluding combinations of groups.

The 9999 permutations are shared with the phi analysis. They are unrestricted in this example; a blocked design or repeated surveys require constraints consistent with the sampling design.

set.seed(123)
nperm <- 499L #to be fast here (better 9999)
indval <- indicspecies::multipatt(
  x = veg,
  cluster = groups$group,
  func = "IndVal.g",
  duleg = TRUE,
  permutations = nperm
)

summary(indval, alpha = 0.05, indvalcomp = TRUE)

The A.g component describes indicator specificity, whereas B describes the frequency of the species within the group. The stat value returned by multipatt() is the square root of IndVal.

6. Phi coefficient

For phi, convert cover values to presence/absence. With func = "r.g", the association is adjusted for unequal group sizes. Occasional species with a cover value of 0.3 are therefore considered present.

veg_pa <- 1L * (veg > 0)

set.seed(123)
phi <- indicspecies::multipatt(
  x = veg_pa,
  cluster = groups$group,
  func = "r.g",
  duleg = TRUE,
  permutations = nperm
)

summary(phi, alpha = 0.05)

Ubiquitous species may have undefined phi values. Keep the phi object with the species names and order of the original matrix, without manually reordering or filtering phi$sign before building the synoptic table.

indval_table <- data.frame(
  species = rownames(indval$sign),
  indval$sign,
  row.names = NULL,
  check.names = FALSE
)
indval_table$group <- levels(groups$group)[indval_table$index]
indval_table$IndVal <- indval_table$stat^2
indval_table$q_BH <- p.adjust(indval_table$p.value, method = "BH")

phi_table <- data.frame(
  species = rownames(phi$sign),
  phi$sign,
  row.names = NULL,
  check.names = FALSE
)
phi_table$group <- levels(groups$group)[phi_table$index]
phi_table$q_BH <- p.adjust(phi_table$p.value, method = "BH")

The q_BH columns provide a separate Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment for each index. The summaries, tb-PCA, and synoptic table in this example follow the interfaces of the functions illustrated and use unadjusted p-values with alpha = 0.05. Keep this distinction explicit when describing the method.

Because groups are derived from the same data, ISA and phi provide an exploratory characterisation of the classification, rather than independent validation or automatic assignment to phytosociological associations.

7. tb-PCA

Compute PCA on Hellinger-transformed cover data. The transformation applies only to the ordination: veg retains the original cover values for classification, ISA, and the synoptic table. Display species selected using phi at alpha = 0.05.

pca <- tb_pca_plot(
  veg = veg,
  groups = groups,
  transformation = "hellinger", # alternative: "chord"
  axes = c(1, 2),
  area = "hull", # "hull", "ellipse", or "none"
  indval = indval,
  phi = phi,
  alpha = 0.05,
  species = "phi", # "indval" or "ordiselect"
  ablim = 0.3,
  fitlim = 0.8,
  freq = FALSE,
  label_groups = TRUE,
  segment.alpha_labelSpe = 0.3,
  segment.size_labelSpe = 0.3
)

pca$plot_sites

pca$plot_species

Convex hulls describe the distribution of surveys in the ordination plane and are not confidence intervals. Interpret the plots alongside the variance explained by the axes and the composition of the groups.

8. Synoptic table

Build the synoptic table from the original cover values and the partition already used for ISA, phi, and PCA. The operational definitions in this example are:

  • diagnostic: phi of at least 0.25 and an unadjusted p-value no greater than 0.05;
  • constant: present in at least 40% of surveys within the group;
  • dominant: cover of at least 25% in at least 50% of surveys within the group.

The last definition corresponds to dominance_rule = "high_cover_frequency". It does not simply mean a mean cover of at least 25% within the group. The three categories may overlap.

stopifnot(
  identical(rownames(phi$sign), colnames(veg)),
  identical(as.character(phi$cluster), as.character(groups$group))
)

tab_sinottica <- synoptic_table(
  veg = veg,
  groups = groups$group,
  phi = phi,
  alpha = 0.05,
  phi_min = 0.25,
  constancy_min = 40,
  dominant_freq_min = 50,
  dominant_cover_min = 25,
  include = c("diagnostic", "constant", "dominant"),
  dominance_rule = "high_cover_frequency"
)

With duleg = TRUE, multipatt() returns the single group with the strongest association for each species. The synoptic table uses that selection for diagnostic species; it does not list all possible species-by-group comparisons. A species may nevertheless be constant or dominant in several groups.

The main table is in long format: a species may appear in multiple rows, one for each group in which it meets the requested category criteria. The frequency matrix includes all species and reports their percentage frequencies within groups.

# Diagnostic species only.
diagnostic_species <- subset(tab_sinottica$synoptic, diagnostic)

9. Optional export

The first chunk saves results and frequencies using base R functions. Both export chunks are excluded from normal rendering.

output_dir <- "risultati_fitosociologia"
dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

write.csv2(groups, file.path(output_dir, "gruppi.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv2(
  group_key,
  file.path(output_dir, "corrispondenza_gruppi.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
write.csv2(
  twinspan_res$results,
  file.path(output_dir, "optimclass.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
write.csv2(indval_table, file.path(output_dir, "indval.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv2(phi_table, file.path(output_dir, "phi.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv2(
  tab_sinottica$synoptic,
  file.path(output_dir, "sinottica_lunga.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

frequency_table <- data.frame(
  species = rownames(tab_sinottica$frequency),
  tab_sinottica$frequency,
  row.names = NULL,
  check.names = FALSE
)
write.csv2(
  frequency_table,
  file.path(output_dir, "frequenze.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

saveRDS(
  list(
    veg = veg,
    optimclass = twinspan_res,
    n.cluster = n.cluster,
    groups = groups,
    group_key = group_key,
    indval = indval,
    phi = phi,
    pca = pca,
    synoptic = tab_sinottica,
    permutations = permutation_matrix,
    parameters = list(
      cut_levels = cut_levels,
      min_size = min_size,
      k_values = k_values,
      p_threshold = p_threshold,
      min_faithful = min_faithful,
      select_by = select_by,
      occasional_cover = occasional_cover
    ),
    session = sessionInfo()
  ),
  file.path(output_dir, "analisi_fitosociologica.rds")
)

If export_synoptic() is also available, export an abbreviated synoptic table to Excel. In the interface used here, min_frequency = 30 retains all diagnostic species and, among the other species in the input synoptic table, those with a frequency of at least 30% in one group. It does not restore species already excluded by include when building the table.

stopifnot(exists("export_synoptic", mode = "function"))

export_synoptic(
  tab_sinottica$synoptic,
  file = "Sinottica_short.xlsx",
  min_frequency = 30,
  digits = 1,
  group_sizes = table(groups$group)
)
